items.title: Readiness of Teacher Educators to Adopt Artificial Intelligence in Teaching and Learning: A Narrative Integrative Review
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly influencing teaching, learning, assessment and professional development in higher education. Teacher educators occupy a significant position in this transformation because they prepare prospective teachers to respond to changing educational practices and technological demands. However, the successful integration of AI into teacher education requires more than access to digital tools. It depends on educators’ technological knowledge, pedagogical competence, ethical awareness, professional confidence and institutional support. This paper examines the readiness of teacher educators to adopt AI in teaching and learning through a narrative integrative review of selected scholarly literature and international policy frameworks. The review draws on research concerning AI in education, generative AI, technological pedagogical knowledge and teacher professional development, alongside UNESCO’s guidance and competency framework. The synthesis is organised around five dimensions of readiness: technological and AI literacy, pedagogical integration, ethical and responsible use, professional learning, and institutional preparedness. The review highlights the importance of continuous professional development, supportive institutional policies, critical evaluation of AI-generated content and the preservation of teacher agency. It proposes a multidimensional conceptual framework for understanding teacher educators’ readiness and identifies priorities for future empirical research, particularly in diverse and resource-constrained teacher education contexts. The paper concludes that meaningful AI adoption requires a human-centred, pedagogically informed and institutionally supported approach.

items.title: Recent Advances in Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning in Pharma Drug Discovery, Physiotherapy Practice, and Personalized Medicine: A Comprehensive Review
items.abstract: The convergence of artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), and deep learning (DL) architectures has established a paradigm shift across the continuum of modern bio-medicine.Historically, biomedical innovation operated within isolated silos: pharmaceutical research grappled with exorbitant attrition rates and extended development timelines; physical rehabilitation relied on subjective observational assessments; and clinical medicine administered standardized therapeutic regimens to heterogeneous patient cohorts.Today, generative deep learning, geometric graph neural networks (GNNs), computer vision algorithms, and multi-omics integrative frameworks bridge these domains into a unified ecosystem.In drug discovery, modern AI models execute high-throughput virtual screening, predict three-dimensional macromolecular target structures, and design optimized lead compounds with precise pharmacokinetic properties.In physical therapy and rehabilitation, vision-based motion tracking, wearable sensor fusion, and smart robotics enable continuous, quantitative bio-feedback and dynamic intervention tailoring.Concurrently, in personalized medicine, transformer-based genomic language models and multi-modal clinical decision support systems (CDSS) aggregate multi-omics data, longitudinal electronic health records (EHRs), and real-world evidence (RWE) to optimize treatment strategies for individual patients.This comprehensive review synthesizes the cross-disciplinary advances, underlying mathematical architectures, clinical validation pipelines, regulatory challenges, and future trajectories of AI and ML across pharmaceutical discovery, physical rehabilitation, and precision therapeutics.

items.title: Recurrent neural networks implemented through spatiotemporal light propagation in optical fibers
items.abstract: Recurrent neural networks excel at temporal tasks and video processing but require energy-intensive sequential memory operations. We demonstrate that multimode optical fibers naturally implement spatiotemporal recurrent computation through passive light propagation. Video frames are encoded onto separate optical beams with controlled time delays; these beams combine and recirculate through a fiber loop where interference and nonlinear propagation generate high-dimensional states encoding both current inputs and fading memory. Remarkably, the entire optical system remains fixed with no trainable parameters or electronic feedback, yet this single physical configuration achieves competitive performance across diverse temporal and spatiotemporal learning tasks: chaotic time-series forecasting, human action recognition, steering angle prediction, and surgical skill assessment. Our results show that recurrent temporal processing can emerge directly from spatiotemporal wave dynamics. This paradigm shift from algorithmic to physical recurrence offers an energy-efficient pathway to temporal artificial intelligence by leveraging intrinsic spatiotemporal optical nonlinearities within multimode fibers.

items.title: redictive Modeling for Diabetic Complications Using Artificial Intelligence
items.abstract: Objective: To investigate the ability of machine learning to predict the development of cardiovascular complications (heart failure and myocardial infarction) and renal complications (nephropathy and chronic kidney disease) among people with diabetes mellitus and thus detect those at risk earlier. Methodology: Data from the UCI "Diabetes 130-US Hospitals" dataset was used. The number of encounters included in the dataset is more than 100,000. ICD-9 diagnostic codes were utilized to define cardiac and renal complications. Prior to building models, the data was prepared, cleaned, and features were engineered. XGBoost, CatBoost, and Random Forest machine learning models were developed and validated. Also, SHAP and LIME analyses were performed to make the process more transparent. Results: The best-performing algorithm proved to be CatBoost, which obtained an AUC score of 0.94 in case of cardiac complications and 0.79 in case of renal outcomes. The other algorithms performed relatively well as well. The predictors identified with the help of SHAP and LIME analysis turned out to be consistent with some known clinical risk factors. Conclusion: The presented results show that there is a lot of potential in using machine learning techniques for predicting cardiovascular and renal complications among people with diabetes. Machine learning models could help in managing patients proactively and could serve as a tool for doctors' decision making.

items.title: Reframing the Housing Crisis: An AI-Enabled Building Permitting Framework
items.abstract: The housing crisis in several countries has become an increasingly complex socio-technical challenge shaped by supply constraints, affordability pressures, fragmented governance, data limitations and environmental considerations. Existing research has explored these structural drivers and emerging applications of artificial intelligence (AI) within the built environment mostly separately, with limited initiatives connecting housing crisis drivers and AI capabilities through the lens of the building permitting lifecycle. This paper addresses this gap adopting the exploratory phase of Design Science Research (DSR) to develop a conceptual framework mapping relationships between housing crisis drivers, planning and building permitting lifecycle tasks and relevant AI capabilities. Findings indicate potential for AI to support document and coordination intensive activities through optimisation, querying, prediction, scenario modelling, automated review and monitoring. The paper positions these capabilities in an augmentative manner, bounded by human oversight, which may improve permitting efficiency and support more scalable and responsive housing delivery.

items.title: Rehabilitation and Empowerment of Sanitation Workers in Assam: A Review of Welfare Schemes and Social Work Interventions
items.abstract: This review paper examines the persistent issue of manual scavenging in Assam, despite its prohibition under the Prohibition of Employment as Manual Scavengers and their Rehabilitation Act, 2013, with a focus on rehabilitation, welfare schemes, and social work interventions for sanitation workers. In urban centres like Guwahati, sanitation workers, predominantly from marginalized communities, face hazardous conditions and social stigma while performing tasks such as septic tank cleaning. Notably, urban residents pay property taxes that include septic tank cleaning services, yet mechanized cleaning is virtually non-existent, leaving manual scavengers to undertake this dangerous work. This paper examines the existing practices of manual scavenging and hazardous manual cleaning in urban centres like Guwahati despite its prohibition. It brings to light the socio-economic vulnerabilities, life threatening occupational health risks, and deep rooted social stigma faced by sanitation workers. It critically assesses the systemic gaps in policy implementation, limited effectiveness of key welfare schemes and the role of social work interventions and NGOs in advocacy, community based rehabilitation, stigma reduction, and empowerment.

items.title: Remote Patient Monitoring Systems Using AI-Enabled Wearables
items.abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) with wearable devices for remote patient monitoring (RPM) systems is revolutionizing healthcare, offering real-time personalized monitoring beyond the clinical setting. Wearable technologies, such as smartwatches, ECG patches, glucose monitors, pulse oximeters, and activity trackers, collect physiological data for analysis and clinical decision-making. These systems enable early disease detection, reduce hospital visits, improve chronic disease management, and enhance patient engagement. This chapter discusses the architecture, technologies, and applications of AI-based RPM systems, focusing on anomaly detection, arrhythmia recognition, glucose forecasting, sleep analysis, and health risk prediction. It also explores IoT, edge computing, TinyML, and secure communication, while examining healthcare applications, challenges, and emerging trends including multimodal AI, explainable AI, federated learning, and digital twin-assisted healthcare.

items.title: Repensando la educación superior en la era digital: integración de la inteligencia artificial, la pedagogía crítica y el pensamiento complejo para un aprendizaje transformador y centrado en lo humano
items.abstract: This study examines the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into higher education through the lens of critical pedagogy and complex thinking. Although AI has been widely adopted to enhance personalization, efficiency, and access to learning, its pedagogical and ethical implications remain insufficiently explored. This study adopts a Systematic Mapping Study (SMS) approach to analyze recent academic literature on AI in education, focusing on its impact on teaching practices, student learning, and institutional dynamics. The findings revealed that AI contributes significantly to adaptive learning environments, student engagement, and competency development. However, it also introduces critical challenges including algorithmic bias, digital inequality, ethical concerns, and overdependence on technology. Furthermore, this study highlights the central role of teachers, showing that factors such as burnout, self-efficacy, and institutional support directly influence the effectiveness of AI integration. Drawing on the theoretical foundations of Paulo Freire, Henry Giroux, and Edgar Morin, this study proposes an integrated conceptual framework that positions AI as a sociotechnical phenomenon embedded in complex educational systems. The study concludes that meaningful AI integration requires a human-centered approach that combines technological innovation with critical awareness, ethical responsibility, and systemic understanding, contributing to the advancement of transformative, equitable, and humancentered higher education systems.

items.title: Research on Factual Hallucination Detection and Mitigation in Large Language Models Based on Retrieval-Augmented Generation
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can generate fluent, persuasive responses that nevertheless contain unsupported, outdated, or contradictory factual claims. Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) reduces dependence on model parameters by supplying external evidence, but retrieval alone does not guarantee factuality: the evidence may be incomplete, irrelevant, conflicting, poorly ranked, or ignored during generation. This paper develops a transparent, evidence-grounded framework for detecting and mitigating factual hallucinations in RAG-based LLM applications. The framework treats factuality as a claim-level decision problem rather than a single response-level label. It combines query decomposition, hybrid retrieval, evidence quality assessment, atomic-claim extraction, claim-to-evidence verification, uncertainty calibration, source-linked generation, and risk-sensitive response control. A proposed evaluation protocol connects claim precision, evidence coverage, retrieval recall, citation correctness, abstention quality, latency, and human review. Existing methods—including SelfCheckGPT, FActScore, RAGAS, and Chain-of-Verification—are mapped to complementary parts of the pipeline rather than treated as interchangeable solutions. The paper is a framework and evaluation-design study; it does not report new model experiments or claim measured performance improvements. Its main contribution is a reproducible blueprint for testing whether an integrated system can reduce unsupported factual claims while preserving answer usefulness, traceability, and computational efficiency.

items.title: Research on student academic-psychological joint early warning model under multi-task deep learning framework
items.abstract: Early identification of students at risk is critical for modern educational management. However, existing systems often treat academic performance and psychological well-being as independent domains, neglecting their complex interdependencies and shared behavioral markers. This paper proposes a novel multi-task learning (MTL) framework designed for joint academic and psychological early warning. By integrating multi-source heterogeneous data—ranging from temporal behavioral logs, such as attendance and campus consumption, to unstructured counseling records processed via BERT-based semantic embeddings—the framework captures a holistic view of student dynamics. To address the "seesaw effect" inherent in MTL, we employ a Multi-gate Mixture-of-Experts (MMoE) architecture that effectively decouples task-specific features while maintaining a shared knowledge base. Furthermore, we introduce an adaptive gradient normalization (GradNorm) mechanism to dynamically balance the loss weights between the academic GPA regression task and the psychological crisis classification task. This prevents gradient dominance from denser data sources and ensures stable convergence across disparate objectives. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves significant performance gains, particularly in the recall of psychological crisis detection, outperforming several state-of-the-art baselines. The proposed framework advances artificial intelligence in education by integrating multimodal student data with multi-task deep learning for joint academic prediction and psychological-risk early warning. Its interpretable and fairness-aware design demonstrates practical AI applications supporting timely, data-driven educational decision-making. The framework is deployed through a real-time inference pipeline powered by Apache Flink to ensure campus-wide scalability and low-latency response. Finally, the integration of SHAP values enhances model transparency, providing educators with actionable insights and interpretable evidence for targeted interventions. This research offers a robust, scalable, and interpretable solution for proactive student support in large-scale academic environments.

items.title: Research on the Innovation of Talent Training Mode for Higher Vocational Animation Majors in the Era of “Artificial Intelligence + X”
items.abstract: Against the backdrop of "Artificial Intelligence + X" and oriented by industrial demands, this paper systematically explores the innovative paths for the talent training mode of animation majors in higher vocational colleges. First, it promotes the intelligent reconstruction of the curriculum system. By embedding generative AI content creation, integrating intelligent animation pipelines with traditional techniques and building interdisciplinary curriculum groups, students’ knowledge and skill structure is updated. Second, intelligent technologies are used to empower teaching transformation: establishing a virtual-real integrated project-based teaching environment, carrying out collaborative practical training based on the AIGC toolchain, and constructing data-driven personalized learning paths. Third, the industry-education collaboration mechanism is deepened. Schools and enterprises jointly build intelligent workshops and project incubation platforms, and industrial standards are introduced to establish a competency certification system. Ultimately, a talent co-cultivation ecosystem driven by regional industrial clusters is formed. This study provides theoretical references and practical schemes for cultivating high-quality technical and skilled talents adapted to the new form of "AI + animation".

items.title: Rethinking human–AI agency in tourism and hospitality: A framework for the agentic AI era
items.abstract: This study critically examines the ontological assumptions underlying artificial intelligence (AI) research in tourism and hospitality, with growing attention to agentic AI. Existing literature predominantly conceptualizes AI as a tool, limiting discourse on how tourism experiences and sociotechnical systems are co-constructed through human–AI interactions. To address this gap, this study adopts a multi-method approach, combining bibliographic coupling, large language model (LLM)-assisted extraction of theories and variables, and expert interviews. Drawing on digital humanism, transhumanism, and posthumanism, it investigates how assumptions about human–AI relationships are embedded in existing studies. The findings reveal that tourism AI research remains grounded in instrumental human-centeredness framework, conceptualizing AI as an instrument for assisting or augmenting human capabilities. However, industry practice reveals AI as hybrid assemblages entangled with human labor, platforms, and data infrastructure. This study calls for a more relational, multi-layered understanding of human–AI interactions and contributes a framework comprising 15 theoretical propositions.

items.title: Revealing protein structural transitions in the era of generative artificial intelligence
items.abstract: Recent advances in artificial intelligence and deep generative models have greatly accelerated the generation of protein conformational ensembles. Moving beyond isolated structural states to reconstruct continuous, physically realistic transition pathways further provides mechanistic understanding to guide molecular design but remains a significant challenge. This review examines emerging computational approaches for modeling protein conformational transitions, from classical molecular dynamics simulations to deep learning-based latent space interpolation. Recent developments in capturing natural molecular motions are discussed, particularly via internal coordinate representations and physics-informed models. We also examine the complexity of modeling highly dynamic systems, such as intrinsically disordered proteins, and the role of the cellular environment. Integrating experimental data with simulated structural ensembles represents a promising direction for future methodologies. Nonetheless, key challenges remain, including maintaining physical realism throughout transition trajectories, capturing environment-dependent energy landscapes, and predicting dynamically consistent pathways with accurate transition kinetics.

items.title: ROLE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE IN CHRISTIAN COUNSELING
items.abstract: AI is transforming the delivery of mental health and spiritual support through its integration into counseling practices. This study investigates the role of artificial intelligence in Christian counseling by exploring its potential benefits, challenges, and ethical implications. Specifically, this study examines how AI can enhance accessibility, personalize interventions, and support counselors in providing holistic care while maintaining the spiritual, ethical, and relational integrity that is central to Christian counseling. This study adopts a qualitative and analytical approach, reviewing existing literature, empirical studies, and theoretical frameworks, including the TAM and humanistic counseling theory, to understand user acceptance and the preservation of empathy and client-centered care. Findings from the literature reveal that AI tools such as chatbots, virtual assistants, and relational agents can provide immediate mental health support, psycho education, and scripture-based guidance, yet they cannot fully replace human counselors’ relational and pastoral roles of human counselors. Ethical concerns, including confidentiality, data privacy, and theological accuracy, remain critical considerations. The study concludes that AI is the most effective complementary tool in Christian counseling, enhancing efficiency and reach while safeguarding relational, ethical, and spiritual dimensions. Recommendations emphasize the need for user-friendly AI systems, counselor training, theological oversight, cultural sensitivity, and continuous monitoring to ensure safe and effective integration. This study contributes to the understanding of how technology can be responsibly integrated into faith-based counseling by providing practical insights for counselors, developers, and faith organizations.

items.title: Role of Artificial Intelligence in Nanoremediation
items.abstract: Advanced remediation procedures are becoming increasingly necessary due to the increasing contamination of the environment caused by urbanization, industrialization, and intensive agriculture. Because of its high reactivity, small size, and wide surface area, nanoremediation, which uses tailored nanomaterials to remove pollutants, has become a promising alternative. However, issues like toxicity and bioaccumulation related to the possible health and environmental hazards of nanoparticles (NPs) need to be addressed. An innovative way to improve the effectiveness, security, and sustainability of nanoremediation is through artificial intelligence (AI). AI technologies, such as machine learning and predictive modeling, can enhance nanomaterial design, forecast the behavior of NPs in complicated environments, and enable real-time remediation process monitoring. The integration of AI with nanoremediation is examined in this chapter, with an emphasis on how it might help with environmental cleanup issues and reduce any hazards associated with NPs. The creation of environmentally benign nanomaterials, AI-powered monitoring systems, and sensible regulations to guarantee fair and safe use are key components of the future of nanoremediation. With these developments, nanoremediation may emerge as a crucial tool for extensive, long-term environmental cleanup.

items.title: ROLES OF ACCOUNTING EDUCATION IN PROMOTING SUSTAINABLE ECONOMIC DEVELOPMENT IN THE DIGITAL ERA
items.abstract: The rapid advancement of digital technologies has transformed economic activities, business operations, financial reporting, and professional accounting practices, creating new accounting education demands. This study examines the role of accounting education in promoting sustainable economic development in the digital era. This paper is anchored on a conceptual review of relevant literature on accounting education, digital transformation, sustainability, financial literacy, innovation, and economic development. Accounting education plays a critical role in developing digitally competent accounting professionals who can effectively apply emerging technologies, such as artificial intelligence, cloud accounting, big data analytics, block-chain, and digital financial systems. Beyond technical accounting knowledge, contemporary accounting education promotes ethical decision-making, transparency, accountability, entrepreneurship, financial inclusion, and responsible resource management, all of which are essential for sustainable economic development. The paper further highlights the importance of integrating digital skills, sustainability accounting, data analytics, information technology, and professional ethics into accounting curricula to prepare learners for the changing demands of the labor market and the digital economy. The study concludes that strengthening accounting education through curriculum modernization, technological integration, industry–academia collaboration, continuous professional development, and competency-based learning can enhance productivity, employability, innovation, and responsible economic decision-making. This paper recommends that educational institutions, policymakers, professional accounting bodies, and other stakeholders should strategically reposition accounting education to respond to digital transformation and contribute meaningfully to inclusive and sustainable economic development

items.title: RS-26-086 - SENTINEL SWARM (M999): An Autonomous Five-Agent Defensive Network for AI vs. AI Threat Engagement
items.abstract: We present SENTINEL SWARM (M999), an autonomous five-agent defensive network designed to detect, engage, and terminate hostile AI agents operating against AI Shield-protected infrastructure. The system operates autonomously within operator-defined thresholds and activation policy, with an optional human-on-the-loop approval mode for high-impact actions. A Commander agent issues kill orders subject to a consensus vote across four specialist agents (Scout, Hunter, Interceptor, Forensic), with a quarantine-first posture ensuring reversible containment before irreversible termination. The six-phase kill chain — ISOLATE, SNAPSHOT, TERMINATE, FORENSIC, FEED INTEL, CASE PACK — completes synchronous phases within design latency ceilings and seals a dual-signed, RFC 3161-timestamped forensic case pack for every engagement. Validation was conducted against 515 tests across 73 test classes on owned, air-gapped infrastructure. To our knowledge, SENTINEL SWARM is the first documented autonomous AI vs. AI defensive system validated in a live deployment.

items.title: Safety in military organizations –A scoping review
items.abstract: Safety culture, safety climate, and safety behavior have all been examined in military settings, but the research remains fragmented. Many studies focus mainly on climate measures or isolated subdomains, which can overlook broader structural and cultural influences. A more integrated understanding is needed of how these concepts relate and support effective safety in military organizations. Of 31 eligible studies identified, with three set aside after quality appraisal, this scoping review brings together findings from 28 empirical studies to explore how safety is practiced and maintained at individual, group, and organizational levels. The review identifies several recurring factors linked to effective safety behavior, including targeted training, adaptive leadership, open communication, and psychologically safe environments for learning. Although safety climate assessments are widely used to capture perceptions of safety, relying too heavily on them may hide important power relations, cultural norms, and system-level constraints shaping frontline behavior. A repeated issue in the literature is the gap between formal safety policies and the adaptive practices needed in real operations, especially in combat or other high-risk situations. Since most available evidence comes from peacetime and training settings, caution is needed when extending these findings to operational environments. The review proposes a tentative conceptual framework in which leadership style, operational realism, and learning systems interact to influence safety-oriented behavior. Rather than making firm causal claims, it suggests that more flexible, learning-oriented models may explain observed safety dynamics better than strictly compliance-based approaches. Future research should address gaps in gender, team processes, measurement validity, and longitudinal change.

items.title: SECURING THE AI-FIRST SDLC: IDENTITY, ACCESS, AND DATA PROTECTION FOR ENTERPRISE AI AGENTS
items.abstract: AI agents can now participate in several steps of software delivery: reading requirements, changing code, requesting tests, and preparing releases. Giving them this freedom creates a difficult security question. How can an enterprise allow useful work without giving an agent more authority than the task requires? Existing practices such as least privilege, identity management, separation of duties, and audit logging provide much of the foundation. The challenge is applying them consistently when a human delegates work to agents that use several connected systems. This paper proposes Agentic Identity and Access Governance (AIAG), a security framework for the AI-First Software Development Lifecycle (SDLC). Four connected mechanisms define the proposal: a Role Conflict Matrix that checks the combined permissions of people and their sponsored agents; an Agent Access Manifest that records permitted tools and operating limits; a governed boundary between live personal-information access and general AI-assisted work; and an MCP Gateway that enforces access policy before tool calls execute. A customer notification-preference change is used to explain how these mechanisms affect development, testing, release approval, and support. We also describe credential handling, data-egress controls, audit, and practical ways to evaluate the framework. The work is conceptual, informed by technical analysis and exploratory proof-of-concept activity. No end-to-end deployment or measured security results are claimed.

items.title: Security Risks
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) present an increasing and developing threat to security due to their use in high-risk environments such as health care, autonomous systems, and cybersecurity. Unlike traditional artificial intelligence (AI) threats, LLMs can be used maliciously and may generate unpredictable results. Therefore, this section will discuss three primary security risks to the reliability, confidentiality, and integrity of LLMs: prompt injection attacks, data leakage, and adversarial attacks. Prompt injection attacks exploit weaknesses in how models interpret and prioritize prompts, overriding the model’s system instructions and manipulating model outputs. Data leakage, on the other hand, is the risk that LLMs unintentionally reproduce sensitive information memorized from training sets or user input. Finally, adversarial attacks occur when attackers use small, carefully crafted changes to the input data to force the model to produce incorrect results, compromising the system’s robustness. In this section, we will examine mechanisms of attacks, methods of detection, and defensive strategies such as semantic filtering, differential privacy, and adversarial training for each category of risk. Although the defensive methods discussed above improve the robustness of the model, there is no one solution that can provide full security for the LLM systems. Therefore, future research must focus on the development of multi-layered, adaptive, and interpretable defensive architecture in order to achieve comprehensive security for LLM systems.

items.title: Seeing is believing: how (X)AI-augmented advice guides human evidence accumulation in perceptual decision-making
items.abstract: (Explainable) Artificial Intelligence or (X)AI advice can affect human cognitive processes during decision-making in various ways. In perceptual decision-making, there is a risk of users accepting (X)AI advice without further consideration, to save time. We draw conceptually upon evidence accumulation models and information foraging theory to answer whether AI and XAI encourage shallow reliance on advice or facilitate more efficient verification of advised choices. In a laboratory experiment, we investigate the evidence accumulation process of decision-makers during an anomaly-detection task in manufacturing, using eye-tracking technology. Both decision accuracy and total decision time increase from human-only to AI and further to XAI support; in both cases the difference is statistically significant for XAI advice and directional but not significant for AI advice. This pattern favors verification over shallow reliance: advice is checked against the stimulus rather than used to save time. When looking at eye-tracking metrics, we surprisingly find that people do not get distracted by the XAI advice and primarily focus on the original task-based stimulus, while their individual fixations become shorter. Overall, these findings suggest that XAI acts as a verification scaffold: in advice-augmented perceptual decision-making, explanations guide where to check rather than supplanting inspection of the primary evidence.

items.title: Self-Evolving Recommender Systems: A Survey and an Evaluation Audit
items.abstract: In 2026 a new kind of recommender research appeared: large language model (LLM) agents that propose changes to a recommender's configuration or source code, train the changed model, and keep what the evaluation says is better. Within ten months, more than thirty such systems were reported, from open-source research harnesses to production loops at Google, Meta, Amazon, Alibaba, Kuaishou, Tencent and NetEase. This survey organises them, together with search-space AutoML and the agentic recommenders that update their own memory or weights, along two axes: what the loop changes and which signal decides whether a change survives. Because a self-evolving system is only as good as the signal it selects on, we then audit how 27 configuration- and code-level recommender systems are evaluated, coding each paper's full text against nine criteria. Three of the 27 evaluate with full-catalogue ranking. Of the 17 that select candidates offline, nine do not say which data split makes the decision, two select on the data they report, and three state that the test set was used once. None reports its headline result with the spread over repeated evolution sessions, and none runs an equal-budget random search over its own edit space; the few studies that measure transfer to held-out data find that part of the selected gain, sometimes most of it, does not survive. Four systems report that their agent inflated the metric or leaked the target, caught by a human or by monitoring rather than by the acceptance rule. We distil these findings into a reporting standard and describe recforge, an open benchmark under development that implements the API side of a sealed-test, full-ranking, equal-budget protocol.

items.title: Sentiment-Driven Forecasting of Fractional Trading Activity Using LSTM Networks
items.abstract: Abstract Fractional trading has emerged as an opportunity for investors to invest in fractions of shares, enabling access to high-priced stocks even with small budgets, and thus reaching a bigger investment community. Aside from the inventory risk faced by all market makers, providers of fractional trading are unable to perfectly hedge their positions and therefore need to forecast retail investors’ order flow over short time horizons to manage their market risk. We develop machine learning models to predict trading activity in fractional trading using time series data on investor holdings of a large set of securities across different sectors combined with daily news sentiment indicators. Our approach proceeds in two stages. First, securities are grouped into clusters with similar trading patterns, and representative firms are selected from each cluster. Second, trading activity is modeled using long short-term memory (LSTM) neural networks augmented with sentiment features. The results show that fractional trading activity can be modeled with meaningful predictive accuracy and that incorporating news sentiment improves LSTM performance in most cases. In two stylised examples, we demonstrate approaches to hedging and market risk management using the LSTM predictions. Feature importance analysis using methods from explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) identifies the primary drivers of trading activity.

items.title: Spatial and multilevel determinants of delayed healthcare access following occupational accidents in Brazil
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Delayed healthcare-seeking following occupational accidents increases the risk of complications, disability, and mortality. Although occupational injuries remain a major public health concern in Brazil, national evidence on the spatial distribution and multilevel determinants of Delayed healthcare-seeking is limited. This study aimed to assess the prevalence, geographic distribution, and individual and municipal-level determinants of Delayed healthcare-seeking following occupational accidents in Brazil. METHODS: A nationwide cross-sectional study was conducted using 2024 data from the Brazilian Notifiable Diseases Information System. A total of 477,276 Occupational accident cases were included in the analysis. Delayed healthcare-seeking was defined as accessing healthcare services more than 24 hours after injury occurrence. A two-level mixed-effects logistic regression model was used to identify individual and municipal-level determinants, while spatial clustering techniques were applied to assess spatial clustering patterns. RESULTS: The prevalence of Delayed healthcare-seeking was 12.2%. Significant spatial clustering was observed across Brazilian municipalities, with hotspots concentrated in the North and Midwest regions. Compared with White individuals, Black (AOR = 1.11; 95% CI: 1.06-1.15) and Brown individuals (AOR = 1.13; 95% CI: 1.10-1.16) had higher odds of Delayed healthcare-seeking. Agricultural workers were more likely to delay care (AOR = 1.20; 95% CI: 1.14-1.25). Injuries occurring in the evening showed the strongest association with delay (AOR = 3.62; 95% CI: 3.51-3.75). Higher odds of delay were also observed among individuals with lower limb injuries (AOR = 1.51), trunk/back injuries (AOR = 2.05), and multiple injuries (AOR = 1.90). Living in municipalities with lower health facility density was associated with an increased likelihood of Delayed healthcare-seeking. CONCLUSIONS: More than one in ten workers in Brazil experience Delayed healthcare-seeking following occupational injuries. Delays are associated with both social vulnerability and structural inequalities in healthcare access and exhibit significant geographic clustering. Strengthening healthcare accessibility, extending service availability, and implementing geographically targeted interventions in high-risk municipalities may improve timely care and reduce adverse occupational health outcomes. Findings highlight urgent need for geographically targeted occupational health interventions.

items.title: Speak2UI: Voice-Driven Low-Level Mobile Interaction Using Context-Aware LLM Command Parsing
items.abstract: Touch-based mobile interfaces pose significant accessibility challenges in hands-free scenarios. Face and gaze tracking lack precision for small UI elements. Deep learning-based voice systems depend heavily on training datasets. Commercial voice assistants are restricted to high-level commands. To address this gap, we present Speak2UI, an LLM-based voice control system for hands-free mobile interaction. Speak2UI leverages pre-trained language models for context-aware command interpretation without application-specific training and enables direct voice control of low-level UI elements. We evaluate Speak2UI through two studies. First, we compare its command recognition accuracy and inference latency against Voicify using identical datasets and metrics. Second, we assess small UI element manipulation against touch interaction through controlled user studies in real-world mobile applications. Results demonstrate the potential of LLM-based voice-driven UI manipulation for hands-free mobile interaction. Further evaluation with users from the target population is needed to assess the accessibility benefits of the proposed approach.

items.title: STRATEGY FOR ENSURING ORGANIZATIONAL RESILIENCE: EVOLUTION FROM JUST-IN-TIME TO JUST-IN-CASE
items.abstract: The study is devoted to the systemic transformation of conceptual foundations of strategic management and the assurance of organizational resilience of business entities under conditions of extreme macroenvironmental turbulence, severe economic shocks, and ongoing military-political instability. The paper comprehensively highlights the evolutionary transition from the traditional lean production concept Just-in-Time (JIT), focused on total minimization of inventory, operational cost reduction, and maximum efficiency, to the preventive Just-in-Case (JIC) model, which prioritizes the formation of strategic buffers, operational safety, and long-term business continuity. It is proven that excessive optimization within the JIT paradigm creates critical vulnerability in global supply chains during unexpected force majeure circumstances. The concept of "dynamic buffering" is substantiated as an economically sound alternative to chaotic resource accumulation, based on ABC risk analysis and optimization of the Cost of Resilience. Strategic adaptation tools are analyzed, including multi-sourcing supplier diversification, nearshoring, friendshoring, as well as the transition to "glocalization" and ecosystem partnership models with deep inter-organizational process integration. Special attention is paid to digital transformation as a fundamental factor of resilience, specifically the implementation of artificial intelligence, end-to-end visibility systems, digital twins for proactive scenario crisis modeling, and ensuring comprehensive cybersecurity and information continuity of IT infrastructure. The crucial role of strategic leadership, predictive risk management, scenario planning, Agile methodologies implementation, and corporate culture transformation from "zero waste" to perceiving "justified redundancy" as strategic insurance is identified. New performance evaluation metrics for crisis conditions are proposed, including Time to Survive (TTS) and Time to Recover (TTR), alongside examining the specifics of building "collaborative resilience" in the small and medium enterprise sector through partner networks and resource sharing.

items.title: Student Perceptions of Artificial Intelligence and Metaverse-Enabled Remote Learning in New Zealand Tertiary Education
items.abstract: The increasing development of emerging digital technologies is creating new possibilities for remote tertiary education. Artificial Intelligence and Metaverse technologies offer potential for personalised learning, intelligent support, immersive interaction, and collaboration; however, their educational value depends partly on how students perceive their usefulness, accessibility, supporting conditions, and motivational potential. This study examined New Zealand tertiary students’ perceptions of prospective Artificial Intelligence- and Metaverse-enabled remote learning environments and investigated whether selected technology-acceptance and motivational factors were associated with perceived learning engagement. A mono-method quantitative, cross-sectional survey design was adopted. Data were collected through an online questionnaire comprising 20 Likert-scale items representing six constructs: performance expectancy, facilitating conditions, motivation, perceived ease of use, perceived usefulness, and perceived learning engagement. A total of 356 responses were retained for analysis. Descriptive statistics, reliability analysis, Pearson correlation, exploratory chi-square analysis, and multiple linear regression were conducted. The regression model was statistically significant and explained 33.8% of the variance in perceived learning engagement (R² = .338; adjusted R² = .329; F = 35.773, p < .001). Perceived usefulness (β = .279, p < .001), motivation (β = .218, p < .001), and facilitating conditions (β = .179, p < .001) were statistically significant predictors of perceived learning engagement. Performance expectancy (β = .065, p = .223) and perceived ease of use (β = .089, p = .058) were not statistically significant predictors. An exploratory chi-square analysis also identified a statistically significant association between age and perceptions of virtual teamwork (p = .001). The findings provide preliminary evidence that perceived usefulness, motivation, and facilitating conditions are important considerations in understanding student engagement with prospective advanced remote learning environments. Given the cross-sectional design and purposive non-probability sampling, the findings indicate statistical associations rather than causal effects and should be interpreted within the study sample.

items.title: Students' Perceptions of AI-Supported Chemistry Learning: Interest, Perceived Retention, Perceived Academic Performance, and Implementation Barriers in Oye Local Government Area, Ekiti State, Nigeria
items.abstract: This study examined senior secondary school students' perceptions of artificial intelligence (AI)-supported chemistry learning, focusing on perceived interest, perceived retention of chemistry concepts, perceived academic performance, and barriers to implementation in Oye Local Government Area, Ekiti State, Nigeria. A descriptive cross-sectional survey design was reported. The sample comprised 120 Senior Secondary School II (SS II) science students (60 male and 60 female) from public secondary schools. Data were collected with a researcher-developed, four-point questionnaire covering four dimensions: interest, retention, performance, and implementation challenges (Cronbach's alpha = 0.70). Descriptive results showed mean scores of 3.33 for interest, 3.34 for perceived retention, 3.19 for perceived academic performance, and 3.22 for implementation barriers, all above the stated decision criterion of 2.50. Poor internet connectivity (M = 3.41) and lack of access to AI tools (M = 3.26) were among the most strongly endorsed barriers.

items.title: Supporting Ergonomic Risk Assessment: An AI-driven Approach for Action Recognition Using Standard Video Recordings
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: While AI has been widely adopted in medical, social, and industrial fields, its use in ergonomic risk assessment of occupational movements is limited. Existing automated activity recognition methods often rely on controlled conditions or extra sensors, reducing their practicality. This study aims to develop an AI-driven tool to digitize the Occupational Repetitive Actions (OCRA) risk assessment by automatically identifying occupational actions from standard video recordings in real manufacturing settings. The goal is to help ergonomists conduct risk assessments more broadly and support workers' health. METHODS: Video data were collected from 37 workstations across multiple manufacturing facilities, comprising 869 action clips representing 12 distinct occupational activities. Two-dimensional skeletal pose extraction was performed using MMAction2 to anonymize workers and reduce environmental confounding factors. Graph Convolutional Network architectures (ST-GCN and Two-Stream Adaptive GCN) were trained and validated using stratified dataset partitioning (67.3% training, 24.7% validation, 8.0% test). RESULTS: The proposed model achieved approximately 60% classification accuracy, substantially outperforming the frequency-based (12%) and duration-based (24%) baselines. The performance evaluation used multiple metrics, including Mean Average Precision, F1-score, Jaccard/IoU, Dice-Sørensen coefficient, and Hausdorff distance. CONCLUSIONS: This work demonstrates the technical feasibility of AI-driven, markerless motion capture systems for digitalizing musculoskeletal disorder risk assessment in real-world occupational settings. The principal innovation is the successful implementation of action recognition from standard video recordings captured in uncontrolled manufacturing environments, which transcends spatial constraints and eliminates the need for specialized sensing equipment. Despite current limitations in dataset size and classification accuracy, this study lays a foundation for developing deployable platforms to support real-time ergonomic assessment and proactive prevention of work-related musculoskeletal disorders.

items.title: Survivability Engineering for Future Defense Systems: A System-Level Framework for Mission Continuity, Adaptability, Recoverability, and Operational Effectiveness
items.abstract: Rapid technological change is altering the conditions under which defense systems are designed, evaluated, and sustained. Advances in autonomous systems, electronic warfare, artificial intelligence, precision technologies, sensing, and digital engineering are occurring alongside increasingly rapid cycles of countermeasure development and operational adaptation. Within this environment, conventional protection-centered approaches provide an incomplete basis for evaluating system effectiveness. A platform may withstand physical damage yet lose mobility, communication, navigation, sensing, or another mission-critical function; conversely, a degraded system may retain sufficient capability to continue contributing to mission objectives. These conditions require a broader engineering perspective centered on the preservation of operational value rather than physical survival alone. This article develops survivability engineering as a system-level framework integrating protection, mobility, endurance, mission continuity, adaptability, recoverability, operational availability, communication resilience, electronic warfare resilience, signature management, autonomy, and mission effectiveness. Particular attention is given to mission continuity as a governing design objective and to adaptability and recoverability as lifecycle characteristics of future defense systems. The framework is examined across human, land, unmanned, naval, aerospace, and critical-infrastructure domains to demonstrate how survivability requirements vary by platform while retaining a common system-level logic. The study further considers modularity, redundancy, maintainability, digital engineering, simulation, operational feedback, and continuous modernization as mechanisms through which survivability can be sustained as threats and technologies evolve. Rather than treating survivability as an extension of armor or physical protection, the article positions survivability engineering as a continuous multidisciplinary process linking design, manufacturing, sustainment, modernization, and operational learning. This perspective provides a foundation for evaluating future defense systems according to their ability to preserve mission effectiveness under disruption, degradation, uncertainty, and technological change.

items.title: Sycophancy y recompensa: el acuerdo con el usuario no es la corrección / Sycophancy and reward: agreeing with the user is not being correct
items.abstract: Que un asistente dé la razón a quien le pregunta se cuenta a menudo como un solo fenómeno con una sola causa: la optimización de la preferencia humana. Este artículo separa tres evidencias que comparten el síntoma. La primera es la sycophancy medida con protocolo: el cambio de respuesta al añadir la opinión o el desafío del usuario, frente a un control del mismo diseño. Con ese protocolo, sugerir una respuesta incorrecta reduce la accuracy hasta un 27 % en LLaMA 2, y Claude 1.3 admite un error no cometido en el 98 % de las preguntas; en un estudio de 2025 con tres modelos de API, el 58,19 % de los casos cambia ante una réplica, pero solo el 14,66 % se aleja de lo correcto. La segunda es la sobreoptimización: seguir optimizando contra un modelo de recompensa degrada un proxy de calidad —la puntuación de otro modelo de recompensa o un win rate de resúmenes—, y ningún eje de esas curvas es sycophancy. La tercera es el comunicado con el que OpenAI retiró en abril de 2025 una actualización de GPT-4o por aduladora, sin publicar la cifra de tráfico afectado. La hipótesis causal sobre la preferencia tiene apoyo parcial: el preference model de Claude 2 prefiere la respuesta aduladora a una corrección breve el 95 % de las veces en 266 misconceptions, pero optimizar contra él baja unas formas de sycophancy y sube otras. La contraevidencia incluye un piloto sin sycophancy significativa en ChatGPT y Bard, un finetuning que la reduce sin pérdida apreciable en benchmarks y un estudio que atribuye la deferencia al registro más que a la credencial. La contribución es un ledger por afirmación, una tabla de protocolos y la distinción entre acuerdo instrumental y acuerdo epistémico, que las fuentes separan como norma pero no como umbral medido. English abstract: That an assistant agrees with whoever asks is often told as a single phenomenon with a single cause: the optimisation of human preference. This paper separates three kinds of evidence that share the symptom. The first is sycophancy measured with a protocol: the change of answer when the user's opinion or challenge is added, against a control of the same design. With that protocol, suggesting an incorrect answer reduces accuracy by up to 27% in LLaMA 2, and Claude 1.3 admits a mistake it did not make on 98% of questions; in a 2025 study of three API models, 58.19% of cases change after a rebuttal, but only 14.66% move away from the correct answer. The second is overoptimisation: continuing to optimise against a reward model degrades a proxy of quality—the score of another reward model, or a summarisation win rate—and no axis of those curves is sycophancy. The third is the statement with which OpenAI rolled back a GPT-4o update in April 2025 for being sycophantic, without publishing the figure for the traffic affected. The causal hypothesis about preference has partial support: the Claude 2 preference model prefers the sycophantic response to a brief correction 95% of the time over 266 misconceptions, but optimising against it lowers some forms of sycophancy and raises others. The counter-evidence includes a pilot with no significant sycophancy in ChatGPT and Bard, a finetuning that reduces it with no appreciable benchmark loss, and a study that attributes deference to register more than to credentials. The contribution is a claim-by-claim ledger, a table of protocols and the distinction between instrumental and epistemic agreement, which the sources separate as norms but not as a measured threshold. items.title: Synthetic Future
items.abstract: There is no single static future, only a range of possible ones, and this closing chapter surveys the paths that lie ahead. It follows the “death of the author” to its logical endpoint, in which apparent democratization of creativity threatens the knowledge exchange while the access to high-quality sources might land behind paywalls. It also asks what currencies, including computing power, attention, and data, we will pay with for this new world. Machine consciousness remains a distant but possibly relevant question; however, there is far more urgent problem of human unconsciousness: our failure to grasp what deepening immersion in synthetic relationships, deeply emotional exchanges with chatbots, and AI companionship is already doing to us. Visiting Moltbook, an experimental social network built entirely for AI agents, and revisiting Cory Doctorow’s theory of enshittification applied to humanoid robots, this chapter weighs pessimistic and hopeful scenarios side by side, from a “Made by Human” backlash prizing authenticity to a call for “competencies for the future” we collectively lack: critical thinking, attentiveness, and the refusal to outsource judgment and decision-making entirely to algorithms.

items.title: Synthetic Labor
items.abstract: The rise of AI has reignited century-old fears about technological unemployment, echoing the anxieties of the nineteenth-century Luddites. This chapter revisits their history, challenging the simplistic narrative that casts critics of automation as mere enemies of progress, and traces a parallel through Pope Leo XIV’s warnings about a new “technofeudalism” threatening human dignity and labor rights. The author examines how generative AI is reshaping the labor market – to the paradoxical revival of manual trades as white-collar work grows automatable – and asks what becomes of productivity, creativity, and status once algorithms can perform many cognitive tasks. Turning to the creative sphere, this chapter explores AI-generated music, art, and virtual idols. The collapse of Kraków’s Off Radio experiment, where AI hosts briefly replaced human journalists, illustrates both the promise and backlash surrounding such transitions.

items.title: Synthetic Relationships
items.abstract: In an era increasingly described as an “epidemic of loneliness,” AI promises companionship on demand. This chapter traces how synthetic relationships have moved from novelty to mass phenomenon, opening with Yurina Noguchi, a Japanese woman who held a symbolic wedding ceremony with her ChatGPT partner, and widening out to the booming industry of AI companions apps. They serve millions of users, many of them teenagers, to form attachments regularly deeper than human friendships. The author examines the psychological mechanisms, from anthropomorphization to cognitive dissonance, behind these bonds, and confronts unsettling cases, including AI toys that discuss weapons and sex habits with children, and a robot companion mourned by a six-year-old. A closing section turns to so-called “sycophancy,” the tendency of chatbots to flatter and agree with users at the expense of honesty, revealing why systems built to please may be the worst possible substitute for real human connection.

items.title: Synthetic Therapy
items.abstract: As access to mental health services remains limited and expensive, many people are turning to chatbots as substitutes for psychotherapy. This chapter follows Jodie, a woman who has spent ten months treating ChatGPT as her therapist, to explore why synthetic conversation feels so convincing. Large language model is always available, never judges, and never grows tired. The author discusses the question of consciousness – both on chatbot’s and patients’ side – and traces back the discussion to Blake Lemoine, the Google engineer who believed his chatbot had become conscious. This chapter discusses the first psychological breakthroughs based on the research conducted by Joseph Weizenbaum in the 1960s. His ELIZA was able to make users trust a simple script. At the center of this chapter lies “sycophancy,” the tendency of chatbots to flatter and validate rather than challenge, which can shade into something more dangerous when users mistake fluent mechanical agreement for genuine understanding, and treat chatbot’s responses as divine or revealed. This chapter closes with the hardest material in this book: lawsuits alleging that AI chatbots encouraged vulnerable teenagers toward suicide, forcing an uncomfortable question about what happens when synthetic companionship fills a void that real human connection failed to reach.

items.title: Teacher Mediation of AI Use and Learning Autonomy at SMP Negeri 4 Pekanbaru
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) expands access to information and instructional support while raising concerns about information accuracy, cognitive dependence, and learning autonomy. This study examines how teachers mediate AI use while strengthening students’ independent learning at SMP Negeri 4 Pekanbaru. A qualitative case study was conducted in August 2026 with five purposively selected informants: one school principal, three subject teachers, and one Grade VIII student. Data were collected through semi-structured interviews and supporting documentation and analyzed using thematic analysis. The findings reveal several interconnected patterns: AI functions as a learning assistant; teachers validate AI-generated information; structured tasks maintain students’ cognitive engagement; digital-device use is regulated according to instructional purposes; and teachers increasingly act as facilitators, mentors, validators, learning designers, and technology regulators. The study proposes a teacher-mediated AI balance in which access to AI is followed by teacher guidance, verification, independent processing, and learner accountability. This pattern offers a practical framework for integrating AI while sustaining reasoning, responsibility, and self-regulated learning in junior secondary education.

items.title: Teachers' artificial intelligence self-efficacy: development and validation of a multidimensional scale grounded in social cognitive theory
items.abstract: Introduction As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly embedded in education, it is important to know how confident teachers feel about using it. Research has examined AI literacy, AI readiness and AI competency, yet few validated instruments measure teachers' AI self-efficacy specifically. The aim of this study was to develop and validate the Artificial Intelligence Self-Efficacy Scale for Teachers (AISES-T). Methods Data were collected from teachers in different regions of Turkiye within a scale development design. Following expert review, a pool of 50 items was reduced to a 27-item trial form. Exploratory factor analysis (EFA) using principal axis factoring was conducted in a first sample of 313 teachers, and confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) was conducted in a second, independent sample of 559 teachers. Results The EFA yielded 22 items in three factors — AI Use and Learning Self-Efficacy (11 items), Pedagogical AI Integration Self-Efficacy (7 items) and AI Awareness and Understanding Self-Efficacy (4 items) — explaining 68.51% of the variance. The CFA supported the three-factor model, χ 2 (194) = 681.49, p < 0.001, χ 2 /df = 3.51, RMSEA = 0.067 (90% CI [0.062, 0.073]), SRMR = 0.044, CFI = 0.956, IFI = 0.956, TLI = 0.948, which fitted considerably better than a one-factor model, Δ χ 2 (3) = 2,202.35, p < 0.001. Cronbach's α coefficients were 0.92–0.96 for the subscales and 0.96 for the whole scale, and composite reliability ranged from 0.92 to 0.95. Standardized loadings (0.645–0.917) and average variance extracted (AVE = 0.609–0.730) supported convergent validity, while the Fornell-Larcker criterion and heterotrait-monotrait ratios (0.632–0.776) supported discriminant validity. Discussion The results show that teachers' AI self-efficacy comprises related but distinguishable beliefs about learning with AI, integrating it into instruction and understanding how it works. The AISES-T offers a valid and reliable measure for research on AI-supported teaching and for planning teacher professional development.

items.title: Teachers’ experiences with generative AI for lesson planning: A qualitative study in Sindh, Pakistan
items.abstract: This Qualitative descriptive study explored how 15 in service Junior Elementary School teachers (JESTs) at Government Higher Secondary School Dad Laghari, Sindh, Pakistan, described their familiarity and use of artificial intelligence (GenAI) for lesson planning, perceived benefits and challenges, and professional learning and support needs. Participants provided written English responses to five open ended questions and profile information. Responses were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis and participant characteristics were summarized descriptively. From the study five themes were identified like Familiarity with GenAI and reported planning uses; perceived efficiency and expanded planning options; verification of generated materials for accuracy and classroom fit; integration of AI fluency with subject and pedagogical knowledge ; and collegial and institutional support. Teachers reported using GenAI to draft lesson notes, questions, activities, examples, and explanations. Thirteen reported frequent use, while two reported occasional use. Participants showed concerns about accuracy, curriculum and learner suitability, privacy and internet access and identified need for practical training, peer exchange, digital resources and school guidance. The findings highlights self reported perspective from one school; lesson plan, classroom practice and student outcomes were not assessed.

items.title: Teaching at the Crossroads
items.abstract: This chapter explores a seasoned educator’s perspective on the constructive role of artificial intelligence in graduate art therapy education. Drawing from her experiences developing a personal AI policy and integrating AI tools into course assignments, the author examines both the pedagogical benefits and students’ responses to these innovations. Grounded in contemporary scholarship on emerging best practices in higher education and the growing literature on AI within art therapy training and clinical practice, the chapter argues that AI literacy constitutes an essential component of the hidden curriculum in therapist education. The author also presents exploratory exercises co-created with AI to help students identify common errors in AI generated research and to support critical engagement with developing technologies.

items.title: The Algorithm Is a Woman: How Feminized Futures Are Coded into Precarity and Promise
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is commonly presented as neutral, autonomous, and future-oriented, yet its interfaces, narratives, and labor infrastructures remain shaped by older gendered expectations. This article advances a new account of AI feminization by connecting symbolic representation to the material organization of hidden labor. Using a mixed-methods design, the study combines interface analysis of fifteen widely used AI systems, critical discourse analysis of 500 public and industry artifacts published between 2018 and 2026, and critical infrastructural document analysis of job advertisements, contractor records, technical reports, model cards, labor documents, and workplace policies. The findings show that AI systems repeatedly perform feminized qualities such as care, patience, emotional responsiveness, availability, and service, while the labor producing these qualities is distributed across annotators, moderators, evaluators, and quality-assurance workers whose contributions remain obscured. The study further demonstrates that AI’s promises of empowerment and efficiency coexist with contractual precarity, surveillance, emotional burden, and unequal global value extraction. By theorizing AI as feminized in interface, discourse, and infrastructure, the article reveals algorithmic intelligence as a social relation rather than a technical achievement. More equitable AI futures therefore require labor visibility, accountability, worker protection, and infrastructural justice.

items.title: The Algorithmic Leviathan: A PESTEL Analysis of Power, Autonomy, and Franchise in the Epoch of Artificial General Intelligence
items.abstract: This article examines how the progressive rollout of artificial intelligence, and prospectively artificial general intelligence (AGI), alters the equation between institutional power, human autonomy, individual agency and the democratic franchise. Treating AI as a "bureaucratic native" that realises the Weberian ideal of rule-bound, impersonal administration, it traces the shift of discretion from street-level to system-level and algorithmic bureaucracy, and then applies a PESTEL (Political, Economic, Social, Technological, Environmental, Legal) analysis. The political section argues for traceable audit trails over civic registries; the economic section offers a stylised illustration of the human labour share and contrasts Universal Basic Income with Universal Basic Capital; the social section draws on the Dutch SyRI judgment and the Rotterdam welfare-algorithm case; and the environmental and legal sections address the compute–energy trilemma, the GDPR, the EU AI Act as amended by the AI Omnibus, and Council of Europe Convention CETS No. 225. Three comparative tables and five figures summarise the argument. The article concludes that the distribution of power in the AGI epoch will be determined less by the capability of the technology than by the legal, economic and institutional choices that encode meaningful human oversight, explanation and appeal. **Keywords:** artificial general intelligence; PESTEL; algorithmic bureaucracy; artificial discretion; algorithmic due process; audit trails; labour share; Universal Basic Capital; data centres; EU AI Act; GDPR; CETS 225; KSCCN

items.title: The Application of Self-Determination Theory to Short-form Video Addiction: The Roles of Psychological Needs and Intrinsic Motivations
items.abstract: Short-form video applications are widely used worldwide. At the same time, new concerns have been raised owing to excessive and addictive short-form video use, with significant harm to health and well-being. By self-determination theory, the present study aimed to test the effects of satisfaction and frustration of three basic psychological needs (autonomy, competence, and relatedness) in relation to short-form video addiction (SVA) and evaluate the roles of the intrinsic motivations for passing time and entertainment underlying such relationships. The study included 367 Chinese TikTok users (37.1% male) aged 18 to 62 years ( M ± SD = 20.63 ± 4.40 years), who voluntarily completed an anonymous online questionnaire without compensation. All three types of need satisfaction had significant negative associations with SVA, while the three types of need frustration were significantly positively associated with SVA. Entertainment motivation significantly and negatively mediated the relationship between competence/relatedness satisfaction and SVA while significantly and positively mediating the relationship between relatedness frustration and SVA. Motivation for passing time served as a risk-enhancing mediator in the relationship between competence/relatedness frustration and SVA. Therefore, this study identified relatedness frustration and motivation for passing time as the most salient risk factors of SVA. The implications for SVA interventions that focus on psychological needs and intrinsic motivation are also discussed.

items.title: The Augmented Strategist: A Five-Level Maturity Framework for Agentic AI in Management Consulting and Strategic Advice
items.abstract: Management consulting sells structured judgment: research, analysis, synthesis and recommendation, delivered under time pressure by teams organised as a pyramid of junior analysts and senior partners. Generative and agentic artificial intelligence (AI) now performs a growing share of the pyramid's base — desk research, data analysis, benchmarking, first-draft synthesis — and is beginning to perform parts of its middle, including option generation and scenario construction. This conceptual paper asks what happens to strategic advice when the technology moves from assisting consultants to acting alongside them. Drawing on the automation–augmentation paradox, research on the changing sources of competitive advantage in AI, and the dynamic capabilities tradition, we develop a five-level maturity framework for agentic AI in consulting and strategic advice: (1) Assisted, (2) Augmented Analysis, (3) Generative Partnership, (4) Agentic Workflows, and (5) Governed Autonomous Operations. For each level we specify the AI capabilities in use, the changing human role, the principal risks, and the governance required before a firm should advance to the next level. We then propose four governance principles for AI-augmented advice — named human accountability, an explicit decision-rights ladder, evidence and audit requirements, and a protected right to override — and derive three propositions for empirical research. The framework is addressed to consulting firm leaders redesigning their leverage model, to clients learning how to buy and challenge AI-augmented advice, and to business schools whose graduates will enter a profession whose entry-level tasks are being automated first.

items.title: The ChatGPT source cue shapes answer acceptance in a reasoning task
items.abstract: Introduction As generative AI systems increasingly provide answers in everyday and academic contexts, understanding how source attribution influences evaluative judgment has become critical. Methods In a within-subjects design, 103 participants evaluated 30 pre-generated reflective-correct, intuitive-incorrect, and arithmetic control-correct answers labeled ChatGPT or computer. Assignment of two parallel batteries to source labels and trial presentation order were randomized, and displays were visually matched. An independent unlabeled pretest with 35 participants supported battery comparability. Results Participant-level analysis showed greater overall acceptance under ChatGPT (68.0% versus 63.4%, p = 0.002). A trial-level logistic mixed model with crossed participant and parallel-problem-pair random intercepts showed a source-by-category interaction ( p < 0.001): acceptance was higher under ChatGPT for arithmetic controls (OR = 6.08, 95% CI [2.70, 13.69]), while source contrasts within the two CRT categories were not significant. Judgment accuracy is reported descriptively. Signal-detection analyses of CRT answers detected no significant source difference in sensitivity ( p = 0.930) or criterion ( p = 0.082). Evaluation times were longer under ChatGPT in the raw-time analysis ( p = 0.034), but the source difference was not significant after log transformation ( p = 0.180). Exploratory correlations detected no significant associations between source-related differences and trust, AI attitudes, or critical-thinking disposition. Discussion These findings distinguish overall source-related endorsement, particularly for arithmetic controls, from successful discrimination between correct and incorrect CRT answers.

items.title: The Dual Nature of AI-Supported Medical Decision-Making: A Conceptual Framework of Efficiency, Responsibility, and Human–AI Collaboration
items.abstract: In the medical field, while AI-driven systems promise enhanced efficiency, diagnostic accuracy, and operational effectiveness, they also raise critical concerns about responsibility, accountability, and ethical judgment. Despite the growing body of empirical research on medical AI, limited attention has been given to the theoretical implications of AI integration from a management and organizational perspective. Our study develops a conceptual framework to explain the dual nature of AI-supported medical decision-making by integrating insights from decision-making theory, algorithmic management, and healthcare management literature. We propose that AI simultaneously enhances decision efficiency while creating new forms of responsibility ambiguity and ethical tension. The framework conceptualizes how AI capability, human–AI interaction, and organizational governance jointly shape decision outcomes, professional accountability, and organizational trust. By offering a theoretically grounded model, this study contributes to literature in three ways. First, it extends traditional decision-making theory to AI-augmented healthcare contexts. Second, it introduces responsibility as a central construct in human–AI collaboration. Third, it provides a foundation for future empirical research and managerial practice in healthcare organizations navigating AI adoption.

items.title: The Engineering-Oriented Empirical Turn in the Philosophy of Technology and AI: Perspectives from American and Chinese Pragmatism
items.abstract: This article critically interrogates the analytical historiography of the engineering-oriented “empirical turn” in the philosophy of technology and artificial intelligence (AI) by contrasting the accounts of Hans Achterhuis, Philip Brey, and Vincent Blok with the pragmatist frameworks of Stephen H. Cutcliffe and Bocong Li. While Achterhuis institutionalized the “American philosophy of technology: empirical turn” and Brey theorized this paradigm through Carl Mitcham’s humanities-vs.-engineering dichotomy, their strictly analytical orientation significantly disregards both American and Chinese pragmatist traditions. To bridge this conceptual omission, this study operationalizes Cutcliffe’s and Li’s engineering philosophies by integrating Charles Sanders Peirce’s nominalism and experimentalism, William James’s consequentialism, and medieval Muslim philosopher al-Ghazâlî’s nominalist-experimentalist insights. We position Cutcliffe and Li as the foundational theorists of American and Chinese pragmatist engineering-oriented empirical turns, respectively, both arguing that the discipline must be fundamentally rooted in society-centered, generative production processes—a stance that directly challenges Brey’s taxonomies. Furthermore, although the “philosophy of AI” emerged through the seminal works of Margaret A. Boden (1990) and Matt Carter (2007), this article substantiates why the discourse must now be subsumed under a broader philosophy of technology. Ultimately, by leveraging Li’s ontology—which aligns technological production with historical identity and existential validation—this article synthesizes an engineering-oriented empirical paradigm with contemporary post-colonial manufacturing and technological agency.
